children.text: evaṃ hi śāstraviṣayo na jijñāsyeta yadi duḥkhaṃ nāma jagati na syāt
children.translated_text: For in this way the subject matter of the treatise would not be something to be inquired into, if there were no such thing as suffering in the world,
or if, though existent, it were not something one wished to abandon,
or if, though one wished to abandon it, it were impossible to eradicate.
The impossibility of eradicating it is twofold:
either because suffering is eternal, or because the means for eradicating it is not known.

children.text: śakyasamucchedatve 'pi ca śāstraviṣayasya jñānasyānupāyatvād vā sukarasyopāyāntarasya sadbhāvād vā
children.translated_text: And even if it can be eradicated, it might be either because the knowledge that is the subject of the treatise is not the means, or because some other easier means exists.

children.text: tatra na tāvad duḥkhaṃ nāsti nāpyajihāsitam ity uktaṃ duḥkhatrayābhighātād iti
children.translated_text: In that regard, first, suffering is not nonexistent, nor is it undesired; this has been stated by the words, 'because of the assault of the threefold suffering.'
The triad of sufferings is the threefold suffering.

children.text: tat khalv ādhyātmikam ādhibhautikam ādhidaivikaṃ ca
children.translated_text: That, indeed, is internal, caused by beings, and caused by divine or unseen forces.
Among these, the internal is twofold: bodily and mental.
The bodily is caused by the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
The mental is based on desire, anger, greed, delusion, fear, jealousy, and the perception of particular objects.
All this is internal suffering, since it is curable by internal means.
Suffering curable by external means is twofold:
that caused by beings and that caused by divine or unseen forces.
Among these, suffering caused by beings is due to humans, domestic animals, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and immobile things.
Suffering caused by divine or unseen forces is based on possession by <s>yakṣas</s>, <s>rākṣasas</s>, <s>vināyakas</s>, planets, and the like.

children.text: tad etat pratyātmani vedanīyaṃ duḥkhaṃ rajaḥpariṇāmabhedo na śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum
children.translated_text: This suffering, experienced in each individual self and being a particular transformation of <s>rajas</s>, cannot be denied.
Thus the hostile connection of this threefold suffering, which abides in the inner organ, with the power of consciousness is the 'assault.'
By so much, its being experienced as adverse, the cause of the wish to abandon it, has been stated.

children.text: yadyapi na saṃnirudhyate duḥkhaṃ tathāpi tadabhibhavaḥ śakyaṃ kartum ityupariṣṭānnivedayiṣyate
children.translated_text: Although suffering is not completely stopped, still its subjugation can be accomplished; this will be explained later.
And accordingly the expression 'in the cause that removes it' is justified.
The remover of that threefold suffering is 'that which removes it.'
Even what is subordinate, when brought close by the intellect at that time, is referred to in this way.

children.text: apaghātakaś ca hetuḥ śāstravyutpādyo nānya ityāśayaḥ
children.translated_text: The intended sense is that the removing cause is one to be taught by the treatise and no other.
Here he raises an objection: 'if the visible means would be pointless.'
The meaning is this:

children.text: astu duḥkhatrayaṃ jihāsatu ca taccetano bhavatu ca tacchakyahānaṃ sahatāṃ ca śāstragamya upāyastad ucchettum
children.translated_text: Let there be the threefold suffering; let the conscious being wish to abandon it; let it be capable of being removed; and let a means known from the treatise be able to eradicate it.
Even so, inquiry into this would not be appropriate for intelligent people,

because there already exists an easy visible means that eradicates it, whereas knowledge of reality is extremely difficult, since it is attainable only through the labor of a succession of practices over many births.
And so there is a popular saying among ordinary people:

children.text: arke cenmadhu vindeta kim arthaṃ parvataṃ vrajet
children.translated_text: 'If one could find honey on the arka plant, why would one go to a mountain?

children.text: iṣṭasyārthasya saṃsiddhau ko vidvān yatnam ācaret ||
children.translated_text: When the desired object is accomplished, what wise person would undertake effort?'
Thus.

children.text: santi copāyāḥ śataṃ śārīraduḥkhapratīkārāyeṣatkarā bhiṣajāṃ varair upadiṣṭāḥ
children.translated_text: And there are hundreds of means for counteracting bodily suffering, easy to perform, taught by the best physicians.
For counteracting mental pain also, the obtaining of pleasant women, drink, food, unguents, clothes, ornaments, and other objects is an easy means.
Similarly, for suffering caused by beings, skill from the study of statecraft, residence in a danger-free place, and the like are easy causes of counteraction.

children.text: tathādhidaivikasya duḥkhasya maṇimantrādyupayogaḥ sukaraḥ pratīkāropāya iti
children.translated_text: Likewise, for suffering caused by divine or unseen forces, the use of gems, mantras, and so on is an easy means of counteraction.
He refutes this:
'No.'
Why?
Because they are absent both with certainty and absolutely.
'Certainty' means the necessary occurrence of the cessation of suffering.
'Absoluteness' means the non-arising again of suffering once it has ceased.
The absence of those two, certainty and absoluteness, is absence with certainty and absolutely.
In the expression 'ekāntātyantataḥ,' the suffix <s>tasi</s>, usable for all cases, stands in place of the genitive.
This is what is meant:

children.text: yathāvidhi rasāyanakāminīnītiśāstrābhyāsamantrādyupayoge 'pi tasya tasyādhyātmikāder duḥkhasyānivṛtter darśanāt anaikāntikatvaṃ nivṛttasyāpi punarutpattidarśanād anātyantikatvam iti sukaro 'pyaikāntikātyantikaduḥkhanivṛtter na dṛṣṭa upāya iti nāpārthā jijñāsetyarthaḥ
children.translated_text: Even when elixirs, women, the study of statecraft, mantras, and the like are used according to rule, since the non-cessation of this or that internal suffering and so on is observed, the remedy is not certain; and since suffering that has ceased is seen to arise again, it is not absolute. Therefore, although easy, no visible means for certain and absolute cessation of suffering exists, and hence inquiry is not pointless. This is the meaning.

children.text: yadyapi duḥkham amaṅgalaṃ tathāpi tadapaghāto maṅgalam eveti yuktaṃ tatkīrtanam iti
children.translated_text: Although suffering is inauspicious, nevertheless its removal is auspicious; therefore the mention of it is proper.

children.text: iti duḥkhavirodhī sukhaviśeṣaḥ svasattayā samūlaghātam apahanti duḥkham
children.translated_text: Thus a particular happiness opposed to suffering, by its own existence, removes suffering with its root.
Nor is this perishable.

children.text: tathā hi śrūyate apāma somam amṛtā abhūmeti
children.translated_text: For it is heard thus: 'We have drunk the soma; we have become immortal.'
If it perishes, how could immortality be possible?

children.text: tasmād vaidikasya tāpatrayapratīkārahetor muhūrtayāmāhorātramāsasaṃvatsarādinirvartanīyatayānekajanmaparaṃparāyāsasaṃpādanīyād vivekajñānād īṣatkaratvāt punar api vyarthā jijñāsetyāśaṅkyāha ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, since a Vedic means for counteracting the three pains is easier than discriminative knowledge, which must be accomplished through the labor of a succession of many births, because it can be carried out in a moment, a watch, a day and night, a month, a year, and so on, one might again object that inquiry is useless; anticipating this, he says:
<s>Anuśrava</s> is the <s>Veda</s>, because it is heard from the recitation of the teacher.
This is what is meant:

children.text: śrūyata eva param na kenacit kriyata iti
children.translated_text: It is merely heard, but it is not performed by anyone.

children.text: tatra bhava ānuśravikas tatra prāpto jñāta iti yāvat
children.translated_text: What is based on that is <s>ānuśravika</s>; that is, what has been obtained there or known there.
Even the scriptural means is like the visible means.
For in both cases there is the same failure to be a means for counteracting suffering certainly and absolutely.

children.text: yadyapyānuśravika iti sāmānyābhidhānaṃ tathāpi karmakalāpābhiprāyaṃ draṣṭavyaṃ vivekajñānasyāpy ānuśravikatvāt
children.translated_text: Although the term <s>ānuśravika</s> is a general designation, it should be understood as referring to the aggregate of ritual acts, since discriminative knowledge too is scriptural.

children.text: tathā ca śrūyata ātmā jñātavyaḥ prakṛtito vivektavyaḥ na sa punar āvartata iti
children.translated_text: And accordingly it is heard: "The self is to be known; it is to be discriminated from <s>prakṛti</s>; then he does not return again."

children.text: asyāṃ pratijñāyāṃ hetum āha sa hyaviśuddhikṣayātiśayayuktaḥ
children.translated_text: With regard to this proposition he states the reason: for that is connected with impurity, decay, and excess.
Impurity is the fact that a soma sacrifice and the like have as their means the killing of animals, seeds, and so on.

children.text: yathāha smātra bhagavān pañcaśikhācāryaḥ svalpaḥ saṅkaraḥ saparihāraḥ sapratyavamarṣa iti
children.translated_text: As the venerable teacher <s>Pañcaśikha</s> has said on this point: "The admixture is slight, removable, and subject to being overpowered."

children.text: svalpaḥ saṅkaro jyotiṣṭomādijanmanaḥ pradhānapūrvasya paśuhiṃsādijanmanānarthahetunāpūrveṇa saparihāraḥ
children.translated_text: The slight admixture arising from a <s>jyotiṣṭoma</s> and the like, whose principal prior potency is born from them, is accompanied by a further potency, born from animal-killing and the like, which causes harm; it is removable.
For it can be removed by some amount of expiation.

children.text: atha pramādataḥ prāyaścittam api nācaritaṃ pradhānakarmavipākasamaye ca pacyate tathāpi yāvad asāv anarthaṃ sūte tāvat sapratyavamarṣaḥ
children.translated_text: But if, through negligence, even the expiation has not been performed, and it ripens at the time when the fruit of the principal act ripens, still, so long as it produces that harm, it is subject to being overpowered.

children.text: mṛṣyante hi puṇyasaṃbhāropanītasudhāhradāvagāhinaḥ kuśalāḥ pāpamātropapāditāṃ duḥkhavahnikaṇikām
children.translated_text: For the virtuous, immersed in a lake of nectar brought about by an accumulation of merit, can endure the small spark of the fire of suffering produced by mere sin.

children.text: na ca mā hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtānīti sāmānyaśāstraṃ viśeṣaśāstreṇāgnīṣomīyaṃ paśum ālabhetetyanena bādhyata iti yuktam
children.translated_text: Nor is it proper to say that the general rule, "One should not injure any beings," is overridden by the special rule, "One should immolate the animal for <s>Agni</s> and <s>Soma</s>."
For there is no contradiction.
Only when there is contradiction is the weaker rule overridden by the stronger.
And there is no contradiction, because their domains are different.

children.text: mā hiṃsyād iti niṣedhena hiṃsāyā anarthahetubhāvo jñāpyate na tvakratvarthatvam api
children.translated_text: For by the prohibition "one should not injure," it is made known that injury is a cause of harm, but not also that it is not for the sake of a sacrifice.
And there is no contradiction at all between being a cause of harm and being helpful to the sacrifice.

children.text: sā hi puruṣasya doṣam āvakṣyati kratoś copakariṣyatīti
children.translated_text: It will bring fault upon the person, and it will assist the sacrifice.
Decay and excess, though belonging to the result, are figuratively attributed to the means.

children.text: kṣayitvaṃ ca svargādeḥ sattve sati kāryatvād anumitam
children.translated_text: And the perishability of heaven and the like is inferred, since, while existent, they are products.
<s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and the like are means only to heaven, while <s>vājapeya</s> and the like are means to sovereignty; thus they are connected with gradation.
For the superiority of another's prosperity makes a person of inferior prosperity suffer.

children.text: apāma somam amṛtā abhūmeti cāmṛtābhidhānaṃ cirasthemānam upalakṣayati
children.translated_text: And the statement "We have drunk soma; we have become immortal" indicates long duration by the word "immortal."

children.text: yad āhur ābhūtasaṃplavaṃ sthānam amṛtatvaṃ hi bhāṣyate
children.translated_text: As they say, "A state lasting until the dissolution of beings is called immortality."
For this very reason there is also the scriptural text:

children.text: na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ
children.translated_text: "Not by action, not by progeny, not by wealth; by renunciation alone some attained immortality.

children.text: pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yad yatayo viśanti ||
children.translated_text: Beyond heaven, lodged in the cave, there shines that which ascetics enter."
Likewise:

children.text: karmabhir mṛtyum ṛṣayo niṣeduḥ prajāvanto draviṇam īhamānāḥ
children.translated_text: "By rites the seers, possessed of offspring and seeking wealth, warded off death.

children.text: tathāpare ṛṣayo manīṣiṇaḥ paraṃ karmabhyo 'mṛtatvam ānaśuḥ ||
children.translated_text: But other thoughtful seers attained immortality beyond ritual acts."
Thus.

children.text: tad etat sarvam abhipretyāha tadviparītaḥ śreyān
children.translated_text: Having all this in view, he says: "The opposite of that is better."

children.text: tasmād ānuśravikād duḥkhāpaghātakād upāyāt somāder aviśuddhād anityasātiśayaphalād viparīto viśuddho hiṃsādisaṅkarabhāvān nityaniratiśayaphalo 'sakṛdapunarāvṛttiśruteḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore, unlike the scriptural means for removing suffering, such as soma rites, which are impure and whose fruit is impermanent and graded, the opposite is pure, because it lacks admixture with injury and the like, and has an eternal, unsurpassed result, since scripture says repeatedly that there is no return.

children.text: na ca kāryatvenānityatā phalasya yuktā bhāvakāryasya tathātvād duḥkhapradhvaṃsasya ca kāryasya tadvaiparītyāt
children.translated_text: And it is not proper that the fruit is impermanent because it is a product, for that is true of a positive product, while the product that is the cessation of suffering is the opposite of that.

children.text: na ca duḥkhāntarotpādaḥ kāraṇāpravṛttau kāryasyānutpādād vivekajñānopajananaparyantatvācca kāraṇasya pravṛtteḥ
children.translated_text: Nor is there the production of another suffering, since, when the cause does not operate, the effect is not produced, and because the operation of the cause lasts only until discriminative knowledge has arisen.
This will be established later.

children.text: akṣarārthastu tasmād ānuśravikād duḥkhāpaghātakāddhetor viparītaḥ sattvapuruṣānyatāpratyayaḥ sākṣātkāro duḥkhāpaghātako hetuḥ
children.translated_text: But the literal meaning is this: therefore, the direct realization consisting in the cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, being the opposite of the scriptural means for removing suffering, is the means that removes suffering.
For this very reason it is better.
For the scriptural means is praiseworthy because it is enjoined by the Veda and because it removes suffering to some extent.
The cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is also praiseworthy.

children.text: tad anayoḥ praśasyayor madhye sattvapuruṣānyatāpratyayaḥ śreyān
children.translated_text: Thus, between these two praiseworthy things, the cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is the better.
Whence, then, does it arise?
For this reason it was said: "from knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower."

children.text: vyaktaṃ cāvyaktaṃ ca jñaśca vyaktāvyaktajñās teṣāṃ vijñānaṃ vivekena jñānaṃ vyaktāvyaktajñavijñānam
children.translated_text: The manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower are the manifest-unmanifest-knower; knowledge of them, knowledge through discrimination, is knowledge of the manifest, unmanifest, and knower.
Knowledge of the unmanifest, its cause, is preceded by knowledge of the manifest.

children.text: tayoḥ pārārthyenātmā paro jñāyata iti jñānakrameṇa kramābhidhānam
children.translated_text: Through the fact that those two exist for another's sake, the self is known as distinct; thus the sequential statement follows the order of knowledge.
This is what is meant:

children.text: śrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇebhyo vyaktādīn vivekena śrutvā śāstrayuktyā ca vyavasthāpya dīrghakālādaranairantaryasatkārasevitād bhāvanāmayāt tattvābhyāsān nāsmi na me nāham ityapariśeṣam aviparyayād viśuddhaṃ kevalam utpadyate jñānam iti
children.translated_text: After hearing from revelation, tradition, epic, and Purāṇa about the manifest and the rest in their distinction, and after establishing them by scriptural reasoning, from the practice of truth, cultivated by meditation over a long time, without interruption and with reverence, there arises pure and absolute knowledge, without error and without remainder: "I am not; nothing is mine; I am not this."

children.text: tad evaṃ prekṣāvadapekṣitārthatvena śāstrārambhaṃ samādhāya śāstram ārabhamāṇaḥ śrotur buddhisamavadhānāya tadarthaṃ saṃkṣepataḥ pratijānīte ||
children.translated_text: Thus, having justified the beginning of the treatise as something whose purpose is desired by the discerning person, the author, beginning the treatise, briefly states its object in order to focus the listener's intellect.
For, in brief, the meaning of the treatise is of four kinds.

children.text: kaścid arthaḥ prakṛtir eva kaścid vikṛtir eva kaścit prakṛtivikṛtiḥ kaścid anubhayaḥ
children.translated_text: One thing is merely a cause; one is merely an effect; one is both cause and effect; one is neither.
Among these, what is the cause?
Hence he says: "<s>prakṛti</s> is not a modification."
Because it produces, it is <s>prakṛti</s>: the <s>pradhāna</s>, the state of equilibrium of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>.
The meaning is: that <s>prakṛti</s> is itself without modification.
Why?
For this reason the word "root" was stated.
It is both root and <s>prakṛti</s>; therefore it is root-<s>prakṛti</s>.

children.text: viśvasya kāryakalāpasya sā mūlaṃ na tvasyā mūlāntaram astyanavasthāprasaṅgāt
children.translated_text: It is the root of the whole aggregate of effects that is the universe, but it has no further root; otherwise an infinite regress would follow.
The idea is that, in an infinite regress, there is no valid means of knowledge.
But which are the prakṛti-vikṛtis, and how many are they?
Therefore it has been said:
The seven, beginning with the great principle, are prakṛti-vikṛtis.
They are both prakṛtis and vikṛtis; thus there are seven prakṛti-vikṛtis.

children.text: tathā hi mahattattvam ahaṃkārasya prakṛtir vikṛtiśca mūlaprakṛteḥ
children.translated_text: For example, the great principle, <s>mahat</s>, is the prakṛti of ahaṃkāra and the vikṛti of root-prakṛti.

children.text: evam ahaṃkāratattvaṃ tanmātrāṇām indriyāṇāṃ ca prakṛtir vikṛtiśca mahataḥ
children.translated_text: In the same way, the principle of ahaṃkāra is the prakṛti of the subtle elements and the senses, and it is the vikṛti of mahat.

children.text: evaṃ pañca tanmātrāṇi bhūtānām ākāśādīnāṃ prakṛtayo vikṛtayaścāhaṃkārasya
children.translated_text: Likewise the five subtle elements are the prakṛtis of the gross elements, beginning with space, and are the vikṛtis of ahaṃkāra.
Now, what is the vikṛti, and how many are there?
Therefore it has been said: but the group of sixteen is a vikāra.
A group measured by the number sixteen is called a ṣoḍaśaka, a group of sixteen.
The word "but" is restrictive, though its position is shifted.

children.text: pañca bhūtānyekādaśendriyāṇīti ṣoḍaśako gaṇo vikāra eva na ca prakṛtiḥ yadyapi pṛthivyādīnām api govṛkṣādayo vikārā evaṃ tadvikārabhedānāṃ payobījādīnāṃ dadhyaṅkurādayastathāpi gavādayo bījādayo vā na pṛthivyādibhyas tattvāntaram
children.translated_text: The group of sixteen, namely the five gross elements and the eleven senses, is only a vikāra and not a prakṛti. Although cows, trees, and the like are also modifications of earth and the other elements, and although curds, sprouts, and the like are similarly modifications of their derivative forms such as milk and seed, still cows and the like, or seeds and the like, are not a different principle from earth and the other elements.
Here being a prakṛti is intended as being the material cause of a different principle; hence there is no fault.

children.text: anubhayam āha na prakṛtir na vikṛtiḥ puruṣa iti
children.translated_text: He states what is neither of the two: puruṣa is neither prakṛti nor vikṛti.
All this will be established below.

children.text: tam imam arthaṃ prāmāṇikaṃ kartum abhimatāḥ pramāṇabhedā darśanīyāḥ
children.translated_text: In order to make this meaning authoritative, the accepted divisions of the means of knowledge must be shown.

children.text: na ca sāmānyalakṣaṇam antareṇa śakyaṃ viśeṣalakṣaṇaṃ kartum iti pramāṇasāmānyaṃ tāvallakṣayati ||
children.translated_text: And since it is not possible to give the special definition without a general definition, he first defines pramāṇa in general.

children.text: atra ca pramāṇam iti samākhyā lakṣyapadaṃ tannirvacanaṃ ca lakṣaṇam
children.translated_text: Here the designation "pramāṇa" is the word for what is to be defined, and its etymological explanation is the definition.

children.text: pramīyate 'neneti nirvacanāt pramāṃ prati karaṇatvaṃ gamyate
children.translated_text: From the explanation "that by which something is known," its instrumentality with respect to true cognition is understood.

children.text: asaṃdigdhaviparītānadhigataviṣayā cittavṛttiḥ bodhaḥ pauruṣeyaḥ phalaṃ pramā tatsādhanaṃ pramāṇam iti saṃśayaviparyayasmṛtisādhanānāṃ pramāṇeṣvaprasaṅgaḥ
children.translated_text: True cognition, pramā, is a mental modification, a cognition concerning an object that is not doubtful, not erroneous, and not already known; its result is personal awareness. The means that produces it is pramāṇa. Thus the causes of doubt, error, and memory do not improperly fall under pramāṇas.
He removes disagreement about their number with the word "threefold."

children.text: tisro vidhā asya pramāṇasāmānyasyeti trividhaṃ na nyūnaṃ nāpyadhikam ityarthaḥ
children.translated_text: This general class of pramāṇa has three varieties; hence it is threefold, neither fewer nor more. That is the meaning.
And we shall establish this after the special definitions.
What are those varieties?

children.text: ata āha dṛṣṭam anumānam āptavacanaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: Therefore he says: perception, inference, and trustworthy verbal testimony.
This is stated with ordinary means of knowledge in view, because the treatise is for instructing ordinary people and has only that as its proper scope.

children.text: ārṣaṃ tu vijñānaṃ yogināṃ na lokapratipādanāyālam iti sad api nābhihitam anadhikārāt
children.translated_text: But the seers' knowledge belonging to yogins, though it exists, is not stated, because it is not adequate for instructing ordinary people and so lies outside the present scope.
One might object:

children.text: mā bhūnnyūnam adhikaṃ ca kasmānna bhavati
children.translated_text: Granted that there are not fewer; but why are there not more?
For disputants do indeed admit comparison and other things also as pramāṇas.
Therefore he says: because all pramāṇas are established within them.

children.text: eṣveva dṛṣṭānumānāptavacaneṣu sarveṣāṃ pramāṇānāṃ siddhatvād antarbhāvād ityarthaḥ
children.translated_text: The meaning is that all pramāṇas are established in, that is, included within, just these: perception, inference, and trustworthy verbal testimony.
And it has been said that this too will be established.

children.text: atha prameyavyutpādanāya pravṛttaṃ śāstraṃ kasmāt pramāṇaṃ sāmānyato viśeṣataśca lakṣayatīti
children.translated_text: But why does the treatise, which has begun in order to explain the knowable object, define pramāṇa both generally and specifically?
Therefore he says: for the establishment of the knowable object is from pramāṇa.
Establishment means apprehension.
This has been explained in accordance with the order of meaning in the āryā verse, disregarding the order of recitation.

children.text: atra dṛṣṭam iti lakṣyanirdeśaḥ pariśiṣṭaṃ tu lakṣaṇam
children.translated_text: Here "perception" is the indication of what is to be defined; the rest is the definition.
The purpose of a definition is to exclude things of the same and of different classes.

children.text: avayavārthastu viṣiṇvanti viṣayiṇam avabadhnanti svena rūpeṇa nirūpaṇīyaṃ kurvantīti yāvat
children.translated_text: But the meaning of the component words is this: objects specify, or delimit, the subject; that is, they make it something to be determined by their own form.

children.text: viṣayāḥ pṛthivyādayaḥ sukhādayaścāsmadādīnām aviṣayāśca tanmātralakṣaṇā yoginām ūrdhvasrotasāṃ ca viṣayāḥ
children.translated_text: Objects are earth and the rest, and pleasure and the rest, for people such as ourselves; and the subtle elements, which are not objects for us, are objects for yogins and beings whose current moves upward.

children.text: viṣayaṃ viṣayaṃ prati vartata iti prativiṣayam indriyam
children.translated_text: A sense faculty that operates with respect to each object is a prativiṣaya sense, an object-by-object sense.
And its operation is contact; the meaning is a sense faculty in contact with its object.
Determination in that means determination based upon it.
And determination is the operation of buddhi, knowledge.

children.text: upāttaviṣayāṇām indriyāṇāṃ vṛttau satyāṃ buddhes tamo'bhibhave sati yaḥ sattvasamudrekaḥ so 'dhyavasāya iti ca vṛttir iti ca jñānam iti cākhyāyate
children.translated_text: When the senses have taken up their objects and their operation is present, and when tamas has been overcome in buddhi, the predominance of sattva that arises is called determination, operation, and knowledge.
This is that pramāṇa.
The assistance thereby given to the power of consciousness has as its result the cognition called pramā.

children.text: buddhitattvaṃ hi prākṛtatvād acetanam iti tadīyo 'dhyavasāyo 'pyacetano ghaṭādivat
children.translated_text: For the principle of buddhi, because it belongs to prakṛti, is unconscious; therefore its determination too is unconscious, like a pot and the like.
Likewise pleasure and the other distinct transformations of the principle of buddhi are also unconscious.
But puruṣa is conscious and is not connected with pleasure and the rest.

children.text: so 'yaṃ buddhitattvavartinā jñānasukhādinā tatpratibimbitas tacchāyāpattyā jñānasukhādimān iva bhavatīti tenānugṛhyate
children.translated_text: This puruṣa, reflected by knowledge, pleasure, and the like existing in the principle of buddhi, through the falling of their shadow, becomes as it were possessed of knowledge, pleasure, and the like; by that it is assisted.

children.text: citicchāyāpattyā cācetanāpi buddhis tadadhyavasāyaśca cetana iva bhavatīti
children.translated_text: And through the falling of the shadow of consciousness, buddhi, though unconscious, and its determination too, become as if conscious.
As he will say:

children.text: tasmāt tatsaṃyogād acetanaṃ cetanāvad iva liṅgam
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of conjunction with that, the unconscious liṅga is as if conscious;
and when the guṇas are the agents, the indifferent one similarly becomes as if an agent.
Thus.
Here, by including the term "determination," he excludes doubt.
For doubt, because it apprehends something unsettled, has an indeterminate form.
Certainty and determination are not different in meaning.
By taking the word "object," he excludes error that has a nonexistent object.
And by taking the prefix "per-," since it indicates contact between sense faculty and object, inference, memory, and the like are excluded.

children.text: tad evaṃ samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakatvāt prativiṣayādhyavasāya iti dṛṣṭasya sampūrṇaṃ lakṣaṇam
children.translated_text: Thus, because it excludes both things of the same class and things of a different class, "determination with respect to each object" is the complete definition of perception.

children.text: lakṣaṇāntarāṇi tairthikānāṃ na dūṣitāni vistarabhayād iti
children.translated_text: The other definitions of the heterodox schools have not been refuted, from fear of prolixity. Thus.

children.text: nānumānaṃ pramāṇam iti vadatā lokāyatikenāpratipannaḥ saṃdigdho viparyasto vā puruṣaḥ pratipādyate
children.translated_text: When the <s>Lokāyatika</s> says that inference is not a pramāṇa, he instructs a person who is either uncomprehending, doubtful, or mistaken.

children.text: na ca puruṣāntaragatā ajñānasaṃdehaviparyayāḥ śakyā arvāgdṛśā pratipattuṃ nāpi mānāntareṇa tadabhāvāt
children.translated_text: But ignorance, doubt, and error residing in another person cannot be known by one whose vision is limited, nor by another means of knowledge, since there is no such means.

children.text: anavadhṛtājñānasaṃśayaviparyāsastu yaṃ kaṃcana puruṣaṃ prati vartamāno 'navadheyavacanatayā prekṣāvadbhir unmattavad upekṣyeta
children.translated_text: But if someone, without having determined ignorance, doubt, or error, addresses just any person, then, because his speech is not worthy of attention, the wise would disregard him like a madman.

children.text: tad anenājñānādayaḥ parapuruṣavartino 'bhiprāyabhedād vacanālliṅgād anumātavyā ityakāmenāpyanumānam abhyupeyam
children.translated_text: Therefore by this, even against his will, inference must be admitted: ignorance and the rest, residing in another person, are to be inferred from speech as a sign, because of a difference in intention.

children.text: tatra pratyakṣakāryatvād anumānaṃ pratyakṣād anantaraṃ nirūpaṇīyam
children.translated_text: Since inference is the effect of perception, it must be explained immediately after perception.

children.text: tatrāpi sāmānyalakṣaṇapūrvakatvād viśeṣalakṣaṇasyānumānasāmānyaṃ tāvallakṣayati liṅgaliṅgipūrvakam iti
children.translated_text: And there too, because the specific definition presupposes the general definition, he first defines inference in general: "preceded by sign and sign-bearer."
The sign is what is pervaded; the sign-bearer is what pervades.

children.text: śaṅkitasamāropitopādhinirākaraṇena svabhāvapratibaddhaṃ vyāpyaṃ yena pratibaddhaṃ tad vyāpakam
children.translated_text: What is pervaded, once suspected or superimposed conditions have been removed, is bound by nature; that by which it is bound is the pervader.
By the mention of sign and sign-bearer, words denoting the object, he indirectly indicates the cognition, the subject directed to that object.

children.text: dhūmādir vyāpyo vahnyādir vyāpaka iti yaḥ pratyayastatpūrvakam
children.translated_text: The cognition that smoke and the like are pervaded, and fire and the like are pervaders, is what precedes it.
And the mention of the sign-bearer must be repeated.

children.text: tena liṅgam asyāstīti pakṣadharmatājñānam api darśitaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: By that, the knowledge that the sign belongs to this, namely knowledge of its being a property of the subject, is also shown.
Thus the general definition of inference has been stated: inference is preceded by knowledge of the pervaded, the pervader, and the sign's being a property of the subject.

children.text: anumānaviśeṣāṃstantrāntare lakṣitān smārayati trividham anumānam iti
children.translated_text: He recalls the particular kinds of inference defined in another system: "inference is threefold."
That which has been defined generally is, specifically, threefold.
It is pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa.
There, first of all, the first is twofold.
It is positive and negative.

children.text: anvayamukhena pravartamānaṃ vidhāyakaṃ vītaṃ vyatirekamukhena pravartamānaṃ niṣedhakam avītam ||
children.translated_text: The positive, proceeding by way of agreement, is affirmative; the negative, proceeding by way of difference, is eliminative.
Among these, the negative is śeṣavat.
The remainder is what remains, what is left over.

children.text: sa eva viṣayatayā yasyāstyanumānasya taccheṣavad yad āhuḥ prasaktapratiṣedhenyatrāprasaṅgācchiṣyamāṇe saṃpratyaya iti
children.translated_text: An inference that has precisely that as its object is śeṣavat; as they say, "conviction arises in what remains, through the negation of what is applicable, because there is no applicability elsewhere."
An example of this negative inference, which proceeds by difference, will be stated later.
And the positive is twofold.
That which has as its object a universal whose own particular instance has been seen is pūrvavat.
"Prior" means previously established, that is, a universal whose own particular instance has been seen.
An inference that has that as its object is therefore pūrvavat.

children.text: yathā dhūmād vahnitvasāmānyasya viśeṣaḥ parvate 'numīyate tasya ca vahnitvasāmānyasya svalakṣaṇaṃ vahniviśeṣo dṛṣṭaṃ rasavatyām
children.translated_text: For example, from smoke a particular instance of the universal firehood is inferred on a mountain; and the own particular instance of that universal firehood, a particular fire, has been seen in a kitchen.

children.text: aparaṃ ca vītaṃ sāmānyatodṛṣṭam adṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇasāmānyaviṣayaṃ yathendriyaviṣayam anumānam
children.translated_text: The other positive inference is sāmānyatodṛṣṭa, having as its object a universal whose own particular instance has not been seen, as in the inference whose object is the sense faculties.

children.text: atra hi rūpādijñānānāṃ kriyātvena karaṇavattvam anumīyate
children.translated_text: For here, cognitions of color and the like, because they are actions, are inferred to possess an instrument.

children.text: yadyapi karaṇatvasāmānyasya chidādau vāśyādi svalakṣaṇam upalabdhaṃ tathāpi yajjātīyaṃ rūpādijñāne karaṇatvam anumīyate tajjātīyasya karaṇatvasya na dṛṣṭaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ pratyakṣeṇa
children.translated_text: Although a particular instance of instrumentality in general, such as an axe and the like in cutting and so on, has been observed, still no particular instance of the same kind of instrumentality as is inferred in cognitions of color and the like has been seen by perception.
For that instrumentality is of the class of the sense faculties.

children.text: na cendriyatvasya sāmānyasya svalakṣaṇaṃ pratyakṣagocaro 'rvāgdṛśāṃ yathā vahnitvasya sāmānyasya svalakṣaṇaṃ vahniḥ
children.translated_text: And for persons whose vision is limited, the particular instance of the universal sense-facultyhood is not within the range of perception, as fire is the particular instance of the universal firehood.

children.text: so 'yaṃ pūrvavataḥ sāmānyatodṛṣṭāt saty api vītatvena tulyatve viśeṣaḥ
children.translated_text: This, then, is the difference between pūrvavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa, even though they are alike in being positive.
Here "seen" means the seeing of the universal as a universal.
The suffix -tas is used with all case meanings.
The meaning is that inference is the seeing of a universal whose own particular instance has not been seen.

children.text: sarvaṃ caitad asmābhir nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkāyāṃ vyutpāditam iti nehoktaṃ vistarabhayād iti
children.translated_text: All this has been explained by us in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s>, and therefore it is not stated here, from fear of prolixity. Thus.

children.text: prayojakavṛddhaśabdasya śravaṇasamanantaraṃ prayojyavṛddhasya pravṛttihetujñānānumānapūrvakatvācchabdārthasaṃbandhagrahasya svārthasaṃbandhajñānasahakāriṇaśca śabdasyārthapratyāyakatvād anumānānantaraṃ śabdaṃ lakṣayatyāptaśrutir āptavacanaṃ tviti
children.translated_text: Because the grasping of the relation between word and meaning is preceded by the inference of knowledge of the cause of action in the elder who is to be prompted, immediately after hearing the words of the elder who prompts; and because a word makes its meaning known with the assistance of knowledge of its relation to its own meaning, after inference he defines verbal testimony: "Trustworthy hearing is trustworthy speech."
"Trustworthy speech" is the indication of what is to be defined; the remainder is the definition.
Āptā means obtained, that is, appropriate or warranted.
Since it is both warranted and śruti, it is āptaśruti, trustworthy hearing.
Śruti is knowledge of a sentence meaning produced by a sentence.

children.text: tacca svataḥpramāṇam apauruṣeyavedajanitatvena sakaladoṣāśaṅkāvinirmuktaṃ yuktaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: And that, being intrinsically valid because it is produced by the authorless Veda, is appropriate, free from every suspicion of defect.
In the same way, knowledge produced by smṛti, itihāsa, and purāṇa that are rooted in the Veda is also appropriate.

children.text: ādividuṣaśca kapilasya kalpādau kalpāntarādhītaśruteḥ smaraṇasaṃbhavaḥ suptaprabuddhasyeva pūrvedyur avagatānām arthānām
children.translated_text: And in the case of <s>Kapila</s>, the first knower, recollection of the Veda learned in another cosmic age at the beginning of the age is possible, just as for one awakened from sleep there is recollection of objects understood on the previous day.

children.text: tathā cāvaṭyajaigīṣavyayoḥ saṃvāde bhagavān jaigīṣavyo daśamahākalpavarti janmasmaraṇam ātmana uvāca daśasu mahāsargeṣu viparivartamānena mayetyādinā saṃdarbheṇa
children.translated_text: Thus too, in the dialogue of <s>Avaṭya</s> and <s>Jaigīṣavya</s>, the blessed <s>Jaigīṣavya</s> spoke of his own recollection of births extending through ten great cosmic ages, in the passage beginning, "by me, revolving through ten great creations," and so on.
By means of trustworthy speech, the pseudo-scriptures of Buddhist monks, Jains, Saṃsāramocakas, and others are rejected as unsuitable.

children.text: ayuktatvaṃ caiteṣāṃ vigānācchinnamūlatvāt pramāṇaviruddhābhidhānāt kaiścid eva mlecchādibhiḥ puruṣāpasadaiḥ paśuprāyaiḥ parigrahād boddhavyam
children.translated_text: And their unsuitability is to be understood from their being disputed, from their having their root cut off, from their stating what contradicts pramāṇa, and from their being accepted only by certain mlecchas and other base men, nearly like animals.
By the word "but" he excludes inference.

children.text: vākyārtho hi prameyaṃ na ca taddharmo vākyaṃ yena tatra liṅgaṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: For the meaning of a sentence is the object to be known; and the sentence is not a property of that meaning, so that it could be an inferential mark there.

children.text: na ca vākyaṃ vākyārthaṃ bodhayat saṃbandhagraham apekṣate
children.translated_text: Nor, when a sentence makes its meaning known, does it depend on the grasping of a relation.
For a sentence composed by a new poet, never seen before, can make known a sentence-meaning never previously experienced.

children.text: evaṃ pramāṇasāmānyalakṣaṇeṣu tadviśeṣalakṣaṇeṣu ca satsu yāni pramāṇāntarāṇyupamānādīnyabhyupeyante vādibhistānyuktalakṣaṇeṣvantarbhavanti
children.translated_text: Thus, when the general definitions of pramāṇa and the special definitions of its kinds have been given, the other pramāṇas, such as comparison and the rest, which are admitted by disputants, are included within the definitions already stated.
For example:

children.text: upamānaṃ tāvad yathā gaustathā gavaya iti vākyam
children.translated_text: Comparison, first of all, is the sentence, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya."
The cognition produced by that is simply verbal testimony.

children.text: yo 'pyayaṃ gavayaśabdo gosadṛśavācaka iti pratyayaḥ so 'pyanumānam
children.translated_text: And the cognition, "This word gavaya denotes something similar to a cow," is also inference.

children.text: yo hi śabdo yatra vṛddhaiḥ prayujyate so 'sati vṛttyantare tasya vācako yathā gośabdo gotvasya
children.translated_text: For whatever word is used by elders with respect to some object, when there is no other function, denotes that object, just as the word "cow" denotes cowness.

children.text: prayujyate caiṣa gavayaśabdo gosadṛśa iti tasyaiva vācaka iti jñānam anumānam eva
children.translated_text: And this word gavaya is used with the meaning "similar to a cow"; therefore the knowledge that it denotes that very thing is inference alone.

children.text: yat tu gavayasya cakṣuḥsaṃnikṛṣṭasya gosādṛśyajñānaṃ tat pratyakṣam
children.translated_text: But the knowledge of similarity to a cow in the case of a gavaya when it is in contact with the eye is perception.

children.text: ata eva smaryamāṇāyāṃ gavi gavayasādṛśyajñānaṃ pratyakṣam
children.translated_text: For that very reason, when a cow is being remembered, the knowledge of the gavaya's similarity to the cow is perception.

children.text: na hyanyad gavi sādṛśyam anyacca gavaye
children.translated_text: For similarity is not one thing in the cow and another in the gavaya.
The connection with many common parts, occurring in one species with respect to another species, is called similarity.

children.text: sāmānyayogaścaikaśced gavaye pratyakṣo gavyapi tatheti nopamānasya prameyāntaram asti yatra pramāṇaṃ bhaved iti na pramāṇāntaram upamānam iti
children.translated_text: And if the connection with the common feature is one and is perceptible in the gavaya, then it is also so in the cow; therefore comparison has no separate object to be known with respect to which it could be a pramāṇa. Thus comparison is not another pramāṇa.
In the same way, presumption too is not another pramāṇa.

children.text: tathā hi jīvataścaitrasya gṛhābhāvadarśanena bahirbhāvasyādṛṣṭasya kalpanam arthāpattir abhimatā vṛddhānām
children.translated_text: For example, the elders hold that presumption is the supposition of <s>Caitra</s>'s unperceived presence outside, from seeing that living <s>Caitra</s> is absent from the house.
That too is inference alone.

children.text: yadā khalu sann ekatra nāsti tadānyatrāsti yadāvyāpaka ekatrāsti tadā nānyatreti sukaraḥ svaśarīre vyāptigrahaḥ
children.translated_text: For when something existent is not in one place, then it is elsewhere; when something non-pervasive is in one place, then it is not elsewhere. The pervasion is easy to grasp in one's own body.

children.text: tathā ca sato gṛhābhāvadarśanena liṅgena bahirbhāvadarśanam anumānam
children.translated_text: Accordingly, by the inferential mark consisting in the perception of the absence from the house of one who exists, the perception of his being outside is inference.

children.text: na ca caitrasya sattvena gṛhābhāvaḥ śakyo 'jñātuṃ yenāsiddho gṛhābhāvo hetuḥ syād gṛhābhāvena vā sattvam apahnūyate yena sattvam evānupapadyamānam ātmānaṃ na bahir avasthāpayet
children.translated_text: Nor is it possible not to know the absence from the house through <s>Caitra</s>'s existence, so that absence from the house would be an unproved reason; nor is existence denied by absence from the house, so that existence itself, being otherwise inexplicable, would not place itself outside.

children.text: tathā hi caitrasya gṛhāsattvena sattvamātraṃ vā virudhyate gṛhasattvaṃ vā
children.translated_text: For is mere existence contradicted by <s>Caitra</s>'s non-existence in the house, or is existence in the house contradicted?

children.text: na tāvad yatrakvacanasattvasyāsti virodho gṛhāsattvena bhinnaviṣayatvāt
children.translated_text: First, existence somewhere or other is not contradicted by non-existence in the house, because the loci are different.

children.text: deśasāmānyena gṛhaviśeṣākṣepo 'pi pākṣika iti samānaviṣayatayā virodha iti cet
children.translated_text: If it is said that, because a particular house is implied by place in general, it is only possible, and therefore there is contradiction through sameness of locus,
no.

children.text: pramāṇaniścitasya gṛhāsattvasya pākṣikatayā sāṃśayikena gṛhasattvena pratikṣepayogāt
children.translated_text: For the non-existence in the house, ascertained by pramāṇa, is capable of rejecting the doubtful existence in the house, since the latter is merely possible.

children.text: nāpi pramāṇaniścito gṛhabhāvaḥ pākṣikam asya gṛhasattvaṃ pratikṣipan sattvam api pratikṣeptuṃ sāṃśayikatvaṃ cāpanetum arhatīti yuktam
children.translated_text: Nor is it reasonable that the house-existence ascertained by pramāṇa, while rejecting his possible existence in the house, should also reject existence itself and remove its doubtful character.

children.text: gṛhāvacchinnena caitrābhāvena gṛhasattvaṃ viruddhatvāt pratikṣipyate na tu sattvamātraṃ tasya tatraudāsīnyāt
children.translated_text: By <s>Caitra</s>'s absence qualified by the house, existence in the house is rejected because it is contradictory, but not mere existence, since it is neutral with respect to that.

children.text: tasmād gṛhābhāvena siddhena sato bahirbhāvo 'numīyata iti yuktam
children.translated_text: Therefore it is reasonable that, from the established absence from the house, the being outside of one who exists is inferred.

children.text: etena viruddhayoḥ pramāṇayor viṣayavyavasthayāvirodhāpādanam arthāpatter viṣaya iti nirastam avacchinnānavacchinnayor virodhābhāvāt
children.translated_text: By this is refuted the claim that the proper object of presumption is the removal of contradiction between two opposed pramāṇas by delimiting their scopes, because there is no contradiction between what is delimited and what is undelimited.
And the other examples of presumption should be included within inference.
Therefore it is established that presumption is not another pramāṇa.
In the same way, absence too is simply perception.

children.text: na hi bhūtalasya pariṇāmaviśeṣāt kaivalyalakṣaṇād anyo ghaṭābhāvo nāma
children.translated_text: For there is no such thing as the absence of a pot apart from the particular transformation of the ground, characterized by isolation.

children.text: pratikṣaṇaṃ pariṇāmino hi sarva eva bhāvā ṛte citiśakteḥ
children.translated_text: Indeed all entities, except the power of consciousness, transform at every moment.

children.text: sa ca pariṇāmabheda aindriyaka iti nāsti pratyakṣānavaruddho viṣayo yatrābhāvāhvayaṃ pramāṇāntaram abhyupeyam iti
children.translated_text: And that difference of transformation is accessible to the senses; therefore there is no object not encompassed by perception for which another pramāṇa called absence would have to be admitted.
Inclusion, for example, is the understanding of a droṇa, āḍhaka, or prastha in a khārī.
That too is inference alone.

children.text: khārītvaṃ hi droṇādyavinābhūtaṃ pratītaṃ khāryāṃ droṇādisattvam avagamayati
children.translated_text: For khārī-ness, known to be inseparably connected with a droṇa and the rest, makes known the existence of a droṇa and the rest in a khārī.

children.text: yaccānirdiṣṭapravaktṛkaṃ pravādamātram iti hocur vṛddhā ityaitihyaṃ yathehavaṭe yakṣaḥ pravasatīti tad apramāṇam anirdiṣṭapravaktṛtvena sāṃśayikatvāt
children.translated_text: And what is mere rumor without a specified speaker, called tradition, as when elders say, "They say that a yakṣa lives in this banyan tree," is not a pramāṇa, because, since the speaker is unspecified, it is doubtful.

children.text: āptapravaktṛtvaniścaye tvāgama ityupapannaṃ trividhaṃ pramāṇam iti
children.translated_text: But when the certainty that the speaker is trustworthy has been established, āgama (authoritative testimony) is also proper; thus the threefold pramāṇa has been established.
Thus, first, the pramāṇas have been defined for the sake of establishing the knowable objects characterized as the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower.

children.text: tatra vyaktaṃ pṛthivyādisvarūpataḥ pāṃsulapado 'pi pratyakṣataḥ pratipadyate pūrvavatā cānumānena dhūmādidarśanād vahnyādīti tadvyutpādanāya mandaprayojanaṃ śāstram iti duradhigamam anena vyutpādanīyam
children.translated_text: Among these, the manifest, in the form of earth and the other elements, is apprehended directly even by a person whose feet are dusty; and by inference of the pūrvavat type, from the sight of smoke and the like, fire and the like are apprehended. Therefore scripture has little purpose for explaining that, and what is difficult to grasp must be explained by it.

children.text: tatra yat pramāṇaṃ yatra śaktaṃ tad uktalakṣaṇebhyo niṣkṛṣya darśayati ||
children.translated_text: There, he extracts from the definitions already stated and shows which pramāṇa is capable with regard to which object.
The word 'but' distinguishes this from perception and pūrvavat inference.

children.text: sāmānyatodṛṣṭād atīndriyāṇām pradhānapuruṣādīnām pratītiściticchāyāpattir buddher adhyavasāya ityarthaḥ
children.translated_text: From inference based on what is generally observed comes the cognition of supersensible things such as <s>pradhāna</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>; the meaning is that determination by buddhi is the assumption of the shadow of consciousness.
And this is an indicative statement.
The inference called śeṣavat should also be understood here.

children.text: tat kim sarveṣvatīndriyeṣu sāmānyatodṛṣṭam eva pravartate
children.translated_text: Then does inference from general observation alone operate with regard to all supersensible things?

children.text: tathā ca yatra tannāsti mahadādyārambhakrame svargāpūrvadevatādau ca teṣām abhāvaḥ prāpta iti
children.translated_text: And, if so, where it is absent, in the sequence of the origination of mahat and the rest, and also in heaven, apūrva, deities, and so on, the non-existence of those things would follow.
Therefore he says, 'and even from that.'

children.text: tasmād apīti siddhe cakāreṇa śeṣavata iti samuccitam
children.translated_text: In the expression 'even from that,' by the particle 'and,' the śeṣavat kind too is included along with what has already been established.
It may be objected:

children.text: yathā gaganakusumakūrmaromanaraviṣāṇādiṣu pratyakṣam apravartamānam tadabhāvam avagamayatyevam pradhānādiṣvapi
children.translated_text: Just as perception, not operating with regard to such things as a flower in the sky, the hair of a tortoise, and a hare's horn, makes known their absence, so too it would do so with regard to <s>pradhāna</s> and the rest.

children.text: tat katham teṣām sāmānyatodṛṣṭādibhyaḥ siddhir iti
children.translated_text: How, then, can their establishment come from inference based on general observation and the like?
Therefore he says:
The word 'non-apprehension,' which is about to be stated, is to be connected by the backward glance of a lion.

children.text: yathotpatan viyati patatrī atidūratayā sann api pratyakṣeṇa anupalabhyate
children.translated_text: For example, a bird flying up in the sky, though present, is not apprehended by perception because of excessive distance.

children.text: sāmīpyād ityatrāpy atir anuvartanīyaḥ yathā locanastham añjanam atisāmīpyānna dṛśyate
children.translated_text: In the phrase 'because of nearness' the word 'excessive' is also to be carried over: for example, collyrium placed in the eye is not seen because of excessive nearness.
Impairment of the sense faculty means blindness, deafness, and the like.

children.text: mano'navasthānād yathā kāmādyupaplutamanāḥ sphītālokamadhyavartinam indriyasaṃnikṛṣṭam apyartham apaśyati
children.translated_text: Because of inattention of the mind: for example, a person whose mind is overwhelmed by desire and the like does not see an object that is in contact with the senses and situated in the midst of abundant light.

children.text: saukṣmyād yathendriyasaṃnikṛṣṭaṃ paramāṇvādi praṇihitamanā api na paśyati
children.translated_text: Because of subtlety: for example, even a person with concentrated mind does not see an atom and the like, though it is in contact with the senses.

children.text: vyavadhānād yathā kuḍyādivyavahitaṃ rājadārādi na paśyati
children.translated_text: Because of obstruction: for example, one does not see the king's wife and the like when separated by a wall or similar barrier.

children.text: abhibhavād yathāhani saurībhir bhābhir abhibhūtaṃ grahanakṣatramaṇḍalaṃ na paśyati
children.translated_text: Because of overpowering: for example, by day one does not see the array of planets and stars overpowered by the rays of the sun.

children.text: samānābhihārād yathā toyadavimuktān udabindūn jalāśaye na paśyati
children.translated_text: Because of being mixed with what is similar: for example, one does not see drops of water released by a cloud in a reservoir.
The particle 'and' has the purpose of collecting what has not been stated.
By it, non-emergence too is included.

children.text: tad yathā kṣīrādyavasthāyāṃ dadhyādyanudbhavān na dṛśyate
children.translated_text: For example, in the state of milk and the like, curds and the like are not seen because they have not yet emerged.
What is meant is this:
The mere cessation of perception does not prove the non-existence of an object, because that would lead to an overextension.

children.text: tathā hi gṛhād vinirgato gṛhajanam apaśyaṃstadabhāvaṃ niścinuyāt
children.translated_text: For, in that case, a man who has gone out from the house and does not see the people of the house would determine their absence.

children.text: api tu yogyapratyakṣanivṛtter ayam abhāvaṃ niścinoti
children.translated_text: Rather, one determines absence from the cessation of a perception that is fit to occur.

children.text: na ca pradhānapuruṣādiṣvasti pratyakṣayogyateti tannivṛttimātrāt tadabhāvaniścayo 'yuktaḥ prāmāṇikānām iti
children.translated_text: But with regard to <s>pradhāna</s>, <s>puruṣa</s>, and the like, there is no fitness for perception; therefore the determination of their absence from the mere cessation of that perception is improper for those who rely on pramāṇas.

children.text: katamat punar eteṣu kāraṇaṃ pradhānādīnām anupalabdhāviti
children.translated_text: Which, then, among these causes accounts for the non-apprehension of <s>pradhāna</s> and the others?
Therefore he says: their non-apprehension is due to subtlety.

children.text: athābhāvād eva saptamarasavad eteṣām anupalabdhiḥ kasmānna bhavatīti
children.translated_text: If it is asked, 'Why should their non-apprehension not be due simply to non-existence, like a seventh taste?'
therefore he says: not because of non-existence.
Why?
Because it is apprehended from its effect.
The word 'it' refers to <s>pradhāna</s>.

children.text: puruṣopalabdhau tu pramāṇaṃ vakṣyati saṃghātaparārthatvād iti
children.translated_text: But with regard to the apprehension of <s>puruṣa</s>, he will state the proof in the phrase 'because the aggregate exists for the sake of another.'

children.text: dṛḍhatarapramāṇāvadhārite hi pratyakṣam apravartamānam ayogyatvānna pravartata iti kalpate
children.translated_text: For when something has been ascertained by a stronger pramāṇa, perception, while not operating, is presumed not to operate because the thing is unsuitable for perception.

children.text: saptamas tu raso na pramāṇenāvadhārita iti na tatra pratyakṣasyāyogyatā śakyādhyavasātum ityabhiprāyaḥ
children.translated_text: But a seventh taste has not been ascertained by any pramāṇa; therefore, in that case, the unsuitability of perception cannot be determined. This is the intended meaning.

children.text: kiṃ punastat kāryaṃ yataḥ pradhānānumānam iti
children.translated_text: What, then, is that effect from which <s>pradhāna</s> is inferred?
Therefore he says:
Mahat and the rest: that is the effect.
And how this is an indicator will be established later.

children.text: tasya ca kāryasya vivekajñānopayoginī sārūpyavairūpye āha prakṛtisarūpaṃ virūpaṃ ca
children.translated_text: And he states the similarity and dissimilarity of that effect, which are useful for discriminative knowledge: it is similar to prakṛti and also dissimilar.
These too are to be analyzed later.
From an effect, merely a cause is known.
And on this point there are disagreements among the disputants.
Some say that the existent is born from the non-existent.

children.text: ekasya sato vivartaḥ kāryajātaṃ na vastu sad ityapare
children.translated_text: Others say that the whole class of effects is a vivarta, an apparent transformation, of the one existent, and is not really existent as an object.
Others, however, say that the non-existent is born from the existent.
The elders say that the existent is born from the existent.

children.text: tatra pūrvasmin pakṣatraye pradhānaṃ na sidhyati
children.translated_text: Among these, in the first three positions, <s>pradhāna</s> is not established.

children.text: sukhaduḥkhamohabhedavacchabdādyātmakaṃ hi jagat kāraṇaṃ pradhānaṃ sattvarajastamaḥsvabhāvam
children.translated_text: For <s>pradhāna</s>, the cause of the world, whose nature is sattva, rajas, and tamas, has the character of sound and the other objects, differentiated as pleasure, pain, and delusion.

children.text: yadi punar asataḥ sajjāyata 'san nirupākhyaṃ kāraṇaṃ sukhādirūpaśabdādyātmakaṃ kathaṃ syāt
children.translated_text: But if the existent were born from the non-existent, how could a non-existent, indescribable cause have the nature of pleasure and the rest and the character of sound and the other objects?
For identity between existent and non-existent is impossible.

children.text: atha sato vivartaḥ śabdādiprapañcas tathāpi sataḥ sajjāyata iti na syāt
children.translated_text: Now, if the manifold of sound and the other objects is a vivarta of the existent, then too it would not be the case that the existent is born from the existent.

children.text: nāsyādvayasya prapañcātmakatvam api tvaprapañcasya prapañcātmatayā bhāsanaṃ bhrāntir eva
children.translated_text: For what is non-dual would not itself have the nature of the manifold; rather, the appearance of what is without manifoldness as having the nature of the manifold would be nothing but error.

children.text: yeṣām api kaṇabhakṣākṣacaraṇādīnāṃ sata eva kāraṇād asato janma teṣām api sadasator ekatvānupapatter akāryātmakaṃ pradhānaṃ sidhyati
children.translated_text: Even for those such as <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> and <s>Akṣacaraṇa</s>, according to whom what is nonexistent is born from a cause that does exist, the pradhāna, which is not itself an effect, is established, because the identity of existent and nonexistent is impossible for them too.

children.text: ataḥ pradhānasiddhyarthaṃ prathamaṃ tāvat satkāryaṃ pratijānīte ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, in order to establish the pradhāna, he first states the thesis that the effect exists.

children.text: sat kāryaṃ kāraṇavyāpārāt prāg iti śeṣaḥ
children.translated_text: The remainder to be supplied is: the effect exists before the operation of the cause.

children.text: tathā ca na siddhasādhanaṃ naiyāyikatanayair udbhāvanīyam
children.translated_text: And thus the sons of the Naiyāyikas should not raise the objection that what is already established is being proved.

children.text: yadyapi ca bījamṛtpiṇḍādipradhvaṃsānantaram aṅkuraghaṭādyutpattir upalabhyate tathāpi na pradhvaṃsasya kāraṇatvam api tu bhāvasyaiva bījādyavayavasya
children.translated_text: Although the arising of a sprout, a pot, and so on is observed after the destruction of a seed, a lump of clay, and the like, still destruction is not the cause; rather, only a positive entity, namely the parts of the seed and so on, is the cause.

children.text: abhāvāt tu bhāvasyotpattau tasya sarvatra sulabhatvāt sarvatra kāryotpādaprasaṅga iti nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkāyām upapāditam asmābhiḥ
children.translated_text: For if a positive entity arose from an absence, since that absence is readily available everywhere, there would follow the production of effects everywhere. This has been explained by us in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s>.

children.text: prapañcapratyaya evāsati bādhake na śakyo mithyeti vaditum iti kaṇabhakṣākṣacaraṇamatam avaśiṣyate
children.translated_text: Thus the view of <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> and <s>Akṣacaraṇa</s> remains: the cognition of the manifest world itself, when there is no defeater, cannot be said to be false.
There this thesis has been stated: the effect exists.
Here he gives the reason: because the nonexistent cannot be made.

children.text: asaccet kāraṇavyāpārāt pūrvaṃ kāryaṃ nāsya sattvaṃ kartuṃ śakyam
children.translated_text: If the effect were nonexistent before the operation of the cause, its existence could not be made.

children.text: na hi nīlaṃ śilpisahasreṇāpi pītaṃ kartuṃ śakyate
children.translated_text: For something blue cannot be made yellow even by a thousand craftsmen.

children.text: sadasattve ghaṭasya dharmāviti cet tathāpyasati dharmiṇi na tasya dharma iti sattvaṃ tadavastham eva tathā ca nāsattvam
children.translated_text: If it is said that existence and nonexistence are properties of the pot, even so, when the property-bearer is absent, that existence cannot be its property; existence remains in the same condition, and consequently nonexistence does not hold.
How can a pot be nonexistent through a nonexistence that is unrelated to it and not identical with it?

children.text: tasmāt kāraṇavyāpārād ūrdhvam iva prāg api sad eva kāryam iti
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as after the operation of the cause, so also before it, the effect certainly exists.
And the making of this already existent effect remains only its manifestation.

children.text: sataścābhivyaktir upapannā yathā pīḍanena tileṣu tailasya avaghātena dhānyeṣu taṇḍulānāṃ dohanena saurabheyīṣu payasaḥ
children.translated_text: And the manifestation of what exists is reasonable, as of oil in sesame seeds by pressing, of rice grains in paddy by threshing, and of milk in cows by milking.

children.text: asataḥ karaṇe tu na nidarśanaṃ kiṃcid asti no khalvabhivyajyamānam utpadyamānaṃ vā kvacid asad dṛṣṭam
children.translated_text: But in the making of what is nonexistent there is no example at all; indeed, nowhere is anything that is being manifested or produced seen to be nonexistent.

children.text: itaśca kāraṇavyāpārāt prāk sad eva kāryam ityāha upādānagrahaṇāt
children.translated_text: For this further reason also the effect exists before the operation of the cause, he says: because a material cause is taken up.

children.text: upādānāni kāraṇāni teṣāṃ grahaṇaṃ kāryeṇa upādānaiḥ kāryasya saṃbandhād iti yāvat
children.translated_text: Material causes are causes; their being taken up means their being taken up by the effect, that is, because the effect is connected with the material causes.

children.text: etad uktaṃ bhavati kāryeṇa sambaddhaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāryajanakam
children.translated_text: What is meant is this: a cause connected with the effect is what produces the effect.
And there is no connection belonging to an effect that is nonexistent.
Therefore it exists.
One might object:

children.text: asaṃbaddham eva kasmāt kāraṇaiḥ kāryaṃ na janyate
children.translated_text: Why is an effect not produced by causes even though it is unconnected with them?
And in that case it will be precisely the nonexistent that arises.
To this he says: because everything would not be impossible, that is, because everything would become possible.

children.text: asaṃbaddhasya janyatve 'saṃbaddhatvāviśeṣeṇa sarvaṃ kāryajātaṃ sarvasmāt sambhavet
children.translated_text: If what is unconnected could be produced, then, since there would be no distinction in being unconnected, every class of effect could arise from everything.
But this is not the case.

children.text: tasmāt sambaddhaṃ sambaddhena janyate yathāhuḥ sāṃkhyavṛddhāḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore what is connected is produced by what is connected, as the elders of Sāṃkhya have said:
If it were nonexistent, there would be no connection with causes that are associated with existence;
and for one who admits the production of what is unconnected, there is no fixed order.
Thus.
One might object:

children.text: asaṃbaddham api tad eva karoti yatra yat kāraṇaṃ śaktam
children.translated_text: Even if unconnected, a cause produces just that effect with respect to which it has capacity.
And capacity is understood from the observation of the effect.
Therefore there is no disorder.
To this he says: because what has capacity makes what is capable of being made.

children.text: sā śaktiḥ śaktakāraṇāśrayā sarvatra vā syācchakye vā
children.translated_text: That capacity, residing in the capable cause, would be either with respect to everything or with respect to what can be made.
If it is with respect to everything, the same disorder remains.

children.text: śakye cet katham asati śakye tatreti vaktavyam
children.translated_text: If it is with respect to what can be made, then it must be said how it is there when the makeable thing is nonexistent.

children.text: śaktibheda eva tādṛśo yataḥ kiṃcid eva kāryaṃ na sarvam iti cet
children.translated_text: If it is said that the very difference of capacity is such that only some particular effect, and not everything, is produced,
well then, sir, is that specific capacity connected with the effect or unconnected?

children.text: sambaddhatve nāsatā saṃbandha iti sat kāryam
children.translated_text: If it is connected, there is no connection with what is nonexistent; therefore the effect exists.

children.text: asaṃbaddhatve saivāvyavastheti suṣṭhūktaṃ śaktasya śakyakaraṇād iti
children.translated_text: If it is unconnected, the same disorder follows. Thus it is well said: because what has capacity makes what is capable of being made.

children.text: itaśca sat kāryam ityāha kāraṇabhāvācca kāryasya kāraṇātmakatvāt
children.translated_text: For this further reason also the effect exists, he says: and because it has the nature of a cause, since the effect is identical in nature with its cause.

children.text: na hi kāraṇād bhinnaṃ kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ ca sad iti kathaṃ tadabhinnaṃ kāryam asad bhavet
children.translated_text: For the effect is not different from the cause, and the cause exists; so how could an effect that is non-different from it be nonexistent?

children.text: kāryasya kāraṇābhedasādhakāni ca pramāṇāni paṭas tantubhyo 'bhidyate
children.translated_text: And the proofs establishing the non-difference of the effect from the cause are these: cloth is not different from threads,
because it is their property.

children.text: iha yad yato bhidyate tat tasya dharmo 'bhavati yathā gaur aśvasya
children.translated_text: Here, whatever is different from something is not its property, as a cow is not a property of a horse.
But cloth is a property of the threads.
Therefore it is not a different entity.
Also because of the relation of material cause and material product, there is no difference of entity between threads and cloth.

children.text: yayor arthāntaratvaṃ na tayor upādānopādeyabhāvo yathā ghaṭapaṭayoḥ
children.translated_text: Where two things are different entities, there is no relation of material cause and material product between them, as between a pot and a cloth.
But there is such a relation of material cause and material product between threads and cloth.
Therefore they are not different entities.
For this further reason also threads and cloth are not different entities:
because there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment.

children.text: arthāntaratve hi saṃyogo dṛṣṭo yathā kuṇḍabadarayoḥ
children.translated_text: For where there is difference of entity, conjunction is observed, as between a jujube and a bowl,
or else non-attainment, as between the <s>Himavat</s> and the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains.
But here there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment.
Therefore they are not different entities.
For this further reason also the cloth is not different from the threads:
because no separate effect of heaviness is apprehended.

children.text: iha yad yasmād bhinnaṃ tasya gurutvāntaraṃ kāryaṃ gṛhyate yathā palikasya rucakasya gurutvakāryo yo 'vanativiśeṣastato dvipalikasya svastikasya gurutvakāryo 'vanatibhedo 'dhikaḥ
children.translated_text: Here, when something is different from something else, a distinct effect of its heaviness is apprehended; for example, compared with the particular downward pull that is the effect of the heaviness of a one-pala ornament, the different downward pull that is the effect of the heaviness of a two-pala svastika ornament is greater.

children.text: na ca tathā tantugurutvakāryāt paṭagurutvasya kāryāntaraṃ dṛśyate
children.translated_text: But in that way no separate effect of the cloth's heaviness is seen apart from the effect of the heaviness of the threads.
Therefore the cloth is non-different from them.
These are the avīta arguments that establish non-difference.

children.text: tad evam abhede siddhe tantava eva tena tena saṃsthānaviśeṣeṇa pariṇatāḥ paṭo na tantubhyo 'rthāntaram
children.translated_text: Thus, when non-difference has been established in this way, the threads themselves, transformed into this or that particular arrangement, are the cloth; the cloth is not a different object from the threads.
The differences of action upon itself, relation, cognition, designation, and practical function cannot establish an invariable difference.
For even in one thing these are not inconsistent, through the manifestation and concealment of this or that particular form.

children.text: yathā kūrmasyāṅgāni kūrmaśarīre niviśamānāni tirobhavanti niḥsaranti cāvirbhavanti na ca kūrmatas tadaṅgānyutpadyante dhvaṃsante vā evam ekasyā mṛdaḥ suvarṇasya vā kuṭakaṭakādayo niḥsaranta āvirbhavanta utpadyanta ityucyate niviśamānās tirobhavanto naśyantītyucyate
children.translated_text: Just as the limbs of a tortoise, when they enter into the tortoise's body, become concealed, and when they come out, become manifest, yet those limbs are not produced from the tortoise nor destroyed, so too, from one and the same clay or gold, pots, bracelets, and the like, when they come forth and become manifest, are said to be produced; when they enter in and become concealed, they are said to perish.

children.text: na punar asatām utpādaḥ satāṃ vā nirodho yathāha bhagavān kṛṣṇadvaipāyanaḥ nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sata iti
children.translated_text: But there is no production of what is nonexistent, nor cessation of what is existent, as the venerable <s>Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana</s> says: there is no being for the nonexistent, and no non-being for the existent.

children.text: yathā kūrmaḥ svāvayavebhyaḥ saṃkocivikāsibhyo na bhinna evaṃ kuṭakaṭakādayo 'pi mṛtsuvarṇādibhyo na bhinnāḥ
children.translated_text: Just as the tortoise is not different from its own contracting and expanding limbs, so pots, bracelets, and the like are not different from clay, gold, and the like.

children.text: evaṃ ca tantuṣu paṭa iti vyapadeśo yatheha vane tilakā ityupapannaḥ
children.translated_text: And thus the designation, "cloth in the threads," is appropriate, just like "tilaka trees here in the forest."
Nor does a difference in practical function entail difference.

children.text: ekasyāpi nānārthakriyādarśanād yathaika eva vahnir dāhakaḥ pācakaśca
children.translated_text: For a single thing is seen to have many practical functions, as one and the same fire burns and cooks.
Nor is the fixed distribution of practical functions a reason for difference of entities.
For those very same things, collectively and separately, are seen to have their fixed practical functions.

children.text: yathā pratyekaṃ viṣṭayo darśanalakṣaṇām arthakriyāṃ kurvanti na śibikāvahanaṃ militāstu śibikāṃ vahantyevaṃ tantavaḥ pratyekaṃ prāvaraṇam akurvāṇā api militā āvirbhūtapaṭabhāvāḥ prāvariṣyanti
children.translated_text: Just as individual bearers perform the practical function characterized by being seen, but not the carrying of a palanquin, while when assembled they do carry the palanquin, so the threads, although individually they do not cover, when assembled and having the state of cloth manifested, will cover.
It may be said:

children.text: āvirbhāvaḥ paṭasya kāraṇavyāpārāt prāk sann asan vā
children.translated_text: Before the operation of the causes, is the manifestation of the cloth existent or nonexistent?
If it is nonexistent, the production of a nonexistent thing follows.
But if it is existent, then what is the use of the making?

children.text: na hi sati kāraṇāṇāṃ vyāpāraṃ paśyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: For we do not observe the operation of causes with regard to what already exists.
And if, in the case of manifestation, one imagines another manifestation, there is the consequence of infinite regress.

children.text: tasmād āvirbhūtapaṭabhāvās tantavaḥ kriyanta iti riktaṃ vacaḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore the statement, "the threads are made into ones in which cloth-state has become manifest," is empty speech.

children.text: athāsad utpadyata iti keyam asata utpattiḥ satī asatī vā
children.translated_text: Now, if it is said that the nonexistent is produced, what is this production of the nonexistent? Is it existent or nonexistent?

children.text: satī cet kṛtaṃ karaṇena asatī cet tatrāpyutpattyantaram ityanavasthā
children.translated_text: If it is existent, what is the use of making? If it is nonexistent, then there too another production must be assumed, and so there is infinite regress.

children.text: athotpattiḥ paṭānnārthāntaram api tu paṭa evāsau tathāpi yāvad uktaṃ bhavati paṭa iti tāvad uktaṃ bhavatyutpadyata iti
children.translated_text: But if production is not a different object from the cloth, but is just that cloth itself, even so, as much as is expressed by the word "cloth" is also expressed by the word "is produced."

children.text: tataśca paṭa ityukta utpadyata iti na vācyaṃ paunaruktyād vinaśyatītyapi na vācyaṃ virodhāt
children.translated_text: Consequently, when "cloth" has been said, "is produced" should not be said, because of repetition; nor should "perishes" be said, because of contradiction.

children.text: tasmād iyaṃ paṭotpattiḥ svakāraṇasamavāyo vā svasattāsamavāyo vā ubhayathāpi notpadyate
children.translated_text: Therefore this production of cloth, whether it is inherence in its own causes or inherence in its own existence, is not itself produced in either case.

children.text: atha ca tadarthāni kāraṇāni vyāpriyanta evaṃ paṭādeḥ sata evāvirbhāvāya kāraṇāpekṣetyupapannam
children.translated_text: And yet causes do operate for that purpose. Thus it is proper that an existent cloth and the like depend on causes for their manifestation alone.
Nor is there a relation of the causes with cloth-form.
For that form is not an action, while causes are related to action; otherwise they would not be causes.
Therefore the thesis that the effect is existent is fully adequate.

children.text: tad evaṃ pradhānasādhanānuguṇaṃ satkāryam upapādya yādṛśaṃ tat pradhānaṃ sādhanīyaṃ tādṛśam ādarśayituṃ vivekajñānopayogi vyaktāvyaktavairūpyaṃ tāvad āha ||
children.translated_text: Thus, having established satkārya, the preexistence of the effect, in a way favorable to the proof of <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), he now states the difference in character between the manifest and the unmanifest, useful for discriminative knowledge, in order to show what sort of <s>pradhāna</s> is to be proved.
The manifest has a cause; "cause" means causal basis, and it possesses that.

children.text: yasya ca yo hetus tad upariṣṭād vakṣyati
children.translated_text: And he will state below what the cause of each thing is.
It is impermanent, that is, destructible, meaning subject to concealment.
It is non-pervasive: everything that is an evolute does not pervade.

children.text: kāraṇena hi kāryaṃ viṣṭaṃ na kāryeṇa kāraṇam
children.translated_text: For the effect is pervaded by the cause, not the cause by the effect.
And buddhi and the rest do not pervade <s>pradhāna</s>; therefore they are non-pervasive.
It is active, meaning possessed of motion.

children.text: tathā hi buddhyādaya upāttam upāttaṃ dehaṃ tyajanti dehāntaraṃ copādadata iti teṣāṃ parispandaḥ
children.translated_text: For buddhi and the rest abandon each body that they have taken up and take up another body; this is their motion.
And the motion of bodies, earth, and the like is well known.
It is many, because buddhi and the rest differ for each <s>puruṣa</s>.
Earth and the rest too are certainly many, because of the differences such as bodies and pots.
It is dependent.
The effect beginning with buddhi depends upon its own cause.

children.text: abhede 'pi kathaṃcid bhedavivakṣayāśrayāśrayibhāvo yatheha vane tilakā ityuktam
children.translated_text: Even though there is non-difference, the relation of support and supported is used with an intended distinction of some sort, as was said in the example, "tilaka trees here in the forest."
It is a liṅga (inferential mark) of <s>pradhāna</s>.

children.text: yathā caite buddhyādayaḥ pradhānasya liṅgaṃ tathopariṣṭād vakṣyati
children.translated_text: And he will state below how buddhi and the rest are a liṅga of <s>pradhāna</s>.

children.text: pradhānaṃ tu pradhānasyāliṅgaṃ puruṣasya liṅgaṃ bhavad apīti bhāvaḥ
children.translated_text: But <s>pradhāna</s> is not a liṅga of <s>pradhāna</s>, though it may be a liṅga of <s>puruṣa</s>; this is the intended meaning.
It is composite.

children.text: avayavanam avayavo miśraṇaṃ saṃyoga iti yāvat
children.translated_text: Avayava, componenthood, means mixture, that is, conjunction.

children.text: aprāptipūrvā prāptiḥ saṃyogastena saha vartata iti sāvayavam
children.translated_text: Conjunction is a contact not previously attained; that which exists together with it is composite.

children.text: tathā hi pṛthivyādayaḥ parasparaṃ saṃyujyanta evam anye 'pi
children.translated_text: Thus earth and the other elements are mutually conjoined, and so too are other things.
But <s>pradhāna</s> is not conjoined with buddhi and the rest, because of identity with them.
Nor is there mutual conjunction among sattva, rajas, and tamas, because there is no prior non-attainment.
Buddhi and the rest are subordinate.
For when buddhi has to produce the effect called ahaṃkāra, it depends upon replenishment from prakṛti.

children.text: anyathā kṣīṇā satī nālam ahaṃkāraṃ janayitum iti sthitiḥ
children.translated_text: Otherwise, being depleted, it would not be capable of producing ahaṃkāra; such is the established position.

children.text: evam ahaṃkārādibhir api svakāryajanana iti sarvaṃ svakārye prakṛtyāpūram apekṣate
children.translated_text: In this way, even by ahaṃkāra and the rest, there is production of their own effects; therefore everything, with respect to its own effect, depends upon the filling in by <s>prakṛti</s>.

children.text: tena prakṛtiṃ parām apekṣamāṇaṃ kāryopajanane paratantraṃ vyaktam
children.translated_text: Therefore the manifest, depending on supreme <s>prakṛti</s> in the production of effects, is dependent on another.
The unmanifest is the opposite of the manifest.

children.text: ahetuman nityaṃ vyāpi niṣkriyaṃ yadyapyavyaktasyāsti pariṇāmalakṣaṇā kriyā tathāpi parispando nāsti ekam anāśritam aliṅgaṃ niravayavaṃ svatantram
children.translated_text: It is without a cause, eternal, pervasive, and inactive. Although the unmanifest has activity characterized by transformation, still it has no motion; it is one, unsupported, without a mark, without parts, and independent.
By this sequence, the dissimilarity of the manifest and the unmanifest has been stated.

children.text: saṃprati tayoḥ sādharmyaṃ puruṣasya ca vaidharmyam āha ||
children.translated_text: Now he states their similarity and the dissimilarity of <s>puruṣa</s>:
It is 'three-guṇed' because the three guṇas, pleasure, pain, and delusion, belong to it.

children.text: tad anena sukhādīnām ātmaguṇatvam parābhimatam apākṛtam
